Comparison: `papers/journal.pdf` vs `simplify.cpp` / `simplify_geometry.h`

## 1. Paper identification

The paper is **"Simplification of Trajectory Streams"** by Siu-Wing Cheng, Haoqiang Huang, and Le Jiang, dated 28 Aug 2025 (uploaded to arXiv as 2503.23025). It is published in this repo at `papers/journal.pdf`.

The implementation in `simplify.cpp` + `simplify_geometry.h` realizes **only the first of the two algorithms presented in the paper**:

- **Implemented**: the streaming **δ-simplification** algorithm (`Algorithm 1: Simplify`, paper PDF lines 361–390, §2, Theorem 3, PDF lines 432–436).
- **NOT implemented**: the streaming **k-simplification** algorithm (`Algorithms 2 & 3: Reduce / Compress`, paper §3.1, Theorem 9, PDF lines 867–876). Despite the README claiming "this repo implements the delta-simplification from the paper" (which is accurate), it is worth noting nothing in `simplify.cpp` corresponds to `Compress`, `Reduce`, the size‑2k boundary, the doubling of δ in `Compress`, or the multi‑run (`blog_{1+ε}(1/ε)` independent runs) machinery required for k‑simplification.

## 2. Theorem being implemented (paper side)

**Theorem 3** (PDF p.8, lines 432–436), restricted to **d = 2**:

> For every δ > 0 and every ε ∈ (0, 1), `Simplify(ε, δ)` outputs a curve σ with
> **d_F(σ, τ) ≤ (1 + ε)δ** and **|σ| ≤ 2κ(τ, δ) − 2**.
> Working storage is **O(ε^(−α))** where α = 2(d−1)⌈d/2⌉² + d → **α = 4 in R²** (so O(ε^(−4))). Per‑vertex processing time is **O(ε^(−α) · log(1/ε)) = O(ε^(−4) · log(1/ε))**.

Supporting invariants: **Lemma 1** (PDF p.5, lines 256–263) — the inductive statement that `S_j[p] = {x ∈ conv(G_{v_j}) : px stabs conv(G_{v_1}), …, conv(G_{v_j}) in order}`; **Lemma 2** (PDF p.7, lines 392–431) — quality and size of σ from concatenating segments.

## 3. Approximation guarantee and the meaning of ε, δ, grid

| Quantity | Paper | Code (`simplify.cpp`) | Where in code |
|---|---|---|---|
| Grid side length (R²) | εδ / (2√d) = **εδ / (2√2)** | `EPSILON * DELTA / (2·√2)` | `GRID_val`, line 135–137 |
| Big‑ball radius | (1 + ε/2)δ | `(1 + EPSILON/2) * DELTA` | `R_val`, line 139–141 |
| Grid cells / "grid points" P | grid cells of Gv that intersect B(x, (1+ε/2)δ) | iterates cells in `[−r/GRID, r/GRID]²`, adds cell corners whenever the cell's nearest corner is inside `B(x, r)` (conservative) | `get_points_from_grid`, lines 156–204 |
| Final Frechet guarantee | d_F(σ, τ) ≤ (1+ε)δ | printed as `Expected Frechet distance` = √(max corner_x² + corner_y²) which is `≤ (1+ε/2)δ + √2 · GRID = (1+ε/2+ε/2)δ = (1+ε)δ` | tracked in `expected_frechet_squared` (line 184–185) and printed at line 491 |
| Curve size | ≤ 2κ(τ, δ) − 2 | the same outer‑loop logic | implicit |

**Critical observation — there is no exact guarantee.** The paper proves only **(1+ε)δ**, and the code is faithful to that proof. The grid discretization step itself inflates the radius from δ to (1+ε/2)δ before intersect (line 224 of paper: `Gv_a` is built from radius (1+ε/2)δ). The remaining ε/2 slack is consumed by linear interpolation between grid corners and the true Frechet match (the "There is a grid point p of G_{v_1} within εδ/2 of x_1" argument in Lemma 2 proof, PDF p.7 lines 421–430).

**Therefore: with or without any heuristic, this implementation cannot promise exact `d_F ≤ δ`.** It is intrinsically an `(1+ε)`‑approximation. There is no constant slack ε you can drop or heuristic you can remove to upgrade it to exact: the approximation slack comes from the grid discretization itself (Lemma 1's dependence on grid‑corner round‑off), not from a heuristic in the code.

## 4. Code paths → paper constructs (one‑to‑one)

| Paper notation | Paper definition | Code location | Lines |
|---|---|---|---|
| `P` (set of grid points in `G_{v_i}`) | §2.1, lines 224–226 | `get_points_from_grid` (returns `std::vector<Point>`) | 156–204 |
| `conv(G_{v_a})` | grid‑cell convex hull covering the ball of radius (1+ε/2)δ | `get_conv_from_grid` (calls CGAL convex_hull_2) | 206–211 |
| `S_a[p]` (inductive state) | `{x ∈ conv(G_{v_a}) : px stabs conv(G_{v_1}),…,conv(G_{v_a}) in order}` | `std::vector<std::vector<Point>> S(Pn)` in `get_longest_stab` | 419, 463–464 |
| `F(S, p)` (the unbounded cone from p through S, "non‑illuminated" region) | §2.1, lines 232–234 | `find_F(p, S, F)` | 259–313 |
| `S_{a+1}[p] = conv(G_{v_{a+1}}) ∩ F(S_a[p], p)` | §2.1, line 230 | `intersect(F[i], Gi, new_S[i])` | `intersect` in `simplify_geometry.h` 548–568 |
| Init `S_1[p] = p` for all p ∈ P | Algorithm 1 line 9 | `for (int i = 0; i < Pn; ++i) S[i] = {P[i]};` | 420 |
| Outer reset on `init=true` when `S_{a+1}[p] = ∅ ∀p` | Algorithm 1 lines 22, 4–9 | loop in `get_longest_stab` lines 428–466 + `if (!has_candidate || dead_cnt == Pn) break;` + `simplify()` calling `get_longest_stab` repeatedly | 461, 477–496 |
| Output segment `(p, q)` where q is a vertex of some non‑empty `S_b[p]` | Algorithm 1 lines 11, 22 | `buffer[0] = P[i]; buffer[1] = new_S[i].front();` (reverse scan, lines 453–459) | 453–474 |

## 5. Implementation choices that diverge from (or go beyond) the paper

### 5.1 Bounding box for `F(S, p)` (a real divergence, but a safe one)
- **Paper (§2.1, lines 232–234):** `F(S, p)` is the **unbounded** cone of points not "illuminated" by S from p — so it has infinitely many bounding halfspaces.
- **Code (`find_F`, lines 259–313):** clips this cone by the **finite axis‑aligned box** `[BMIN, BMAX]²` via `current_bbox()` and `append_rect_pts`. The box is computed in `configure_bbox` (lines 143–154) to contain `min/max(stream) ± (R + GRID·√2 + padding)`, so the box is large enough to enclose every `conv(G_{v_a})` ever constructed.

This is a **pragmatic approximation that does not weaken Theorem 3**, because every point of every `conv(G_{v_a})` lies well inside the box, so the intersection with the (clipped) cone still produces the exact same polygon for the purpose of Lemma 1. It does, however, give `F` a finite number of vertices (`n + 4` reserved at line 293), which is necessary for the O(ε^(−4)) complexity bound to hold concretely.

### 5.2 Cell‑corner test in `get_points_from_grid` (lines 189–201)
- **Paper:** "grid cells that intersect `B(x, (1+ε/2)δ)`" — defined in §2 line 209.
- **Code:** iterates cells whose **nearest corner** lies within `B(x, r)` with r = (1+ε/2)δ, then adds all four cell corners. This is a slightly conservative superset of the paper's set — the paper's condition is "cell intersects the ball", which is *equivalent* to "the cell's nearest point to x lies in the ball". So the sets match exactly.

### 5.3 Pick of `q` (the output endpoint) (lines 453–459)
- **Paper, Algorithm 1 line 11:** "choose any vertex q of some non‑empty Si[p]" — completely arbitrary.
- **Code:** iterates `i` from `Pn−1` down to `0`, takes the first non‑dead `i` with non‑empty `new_S[i]`, and sets `q = new_S[i].front()`. This deterministically picks the "last surviving" (in index order) polytope and its first stored vertex. Still satisfies Lemma 1(i) — that vertex lies inside `S_{a+1}[p] ⊆ conv(G_{v_{a+1}})`.

### 5.4 The `expected_frechet_squared` global (lines 23, 184–185, 491)
- This is a **diagnostic printout only**, not a heuristic. It tracks the maximum squared radius reached by any grid corner (≤ (1+ε/2)δ + GRID·√2/2 · √2 = (1+ε/2 + ε/2)δ = (1+ε)δ). It is **not** used in any control‑flow decision.

### 5.5 Numerical / kernel concerns
- The header (`simplify_geometry.h` lines 18–24) uses `Epick = Exact_predicates_inexact_constructions_kernel` for orientation/sign tests (exact) and double arithmetic for intersection points. This is fine for Theorem 3 because the proof is purely about combinatorial/structural correctness (Lemma 1's inductive equivalence) and the final Frechet bound is dominated by the grid slack, not double round‑off. The "robust" Sutherland–Hodgman branch at lines 281–450 of `simplify_geometry.h` even falls back to CGAL's exact `Line_2` intersection when the raw double is ambiguous.

### 5.6 `assert(S.size() != 2)` in `find_F` (line 262)
- The paper never analyzes the |S| = 2 case (Lemma 1 assumes S_a is a convex polytope of dim ≥ 2). The code asserts this never happens; if it does, `find_F` returns with `F` empty (silent fallthrough to line 270). In practice this is unreachable because `S_a[p]` always has at least the conv hull of G_{v_a} if non‑empty, which has ≥ 3 vertices.

### 5.7 Rounding/Frechet verification path
- The `--dist` flag (line 599 of `simplify.cpp`) shells out to `scripts/frechet` (a Julia wrapper around `FrechetDist.jl`), used purely for empirical benchmarking. It does **not** affect the algorithm or its guarantees.

## 6. Bottom line: can this code promise exact `d_F ≤ δ`?

**No.** And this is true with or without any heuristic — the (1+ε) slack is structural, not heuristic:

1. The algorithm covers each ball of radius δ around `v_a` with `conv(G_{v_a})`, where `G_{v_a}` is defined using **radius (1+ε/2)δ** (paper §2, line 210; code line 139–141 `R_val`).
2. The grid corners are offset by up to `√2 · GRID/2 = εδ/2` from the continuous ball boundary (paper §2.2 Lemma 2 proof, PDF p.7 lines 421–430).
3. Adding these two slacks gives `(1+ε/2)δ + εδ/2 = (1+ε)δ`.

**Removing the heuristic (there is none to remove) does not change the answer.** To get an *exact* `d_F ≤ δ` you would have to switch to a non‑approximate algorithm — e.g., the static O(n² log²n) minimum‑link path algorithm of Guibas et al. [16] cited in the paper's §1.1 — which is **not streaming**, which is exactly why the paper develops the (1+ε) streaming version in the first place.

So the implementation honestly matches Theorem 3's `(1+ε)δ` guarantee with no hidden degradation.

## 7. Missing implementation work needed for full paper fidelity

If you want to extend `simplify.cpp` to match **all** of the paper's stated guarantees, the missing piece is the **k‑simplification** algorithm (§3.1, Algorithms 2 & 3, Theorem 9):

1. Add the `δmin` initial lower bound (Lemma 4, PDF p.11 lines 675–688, applied at line 3 of `Reduce`).
2. Add the `Compress` subroutine that invokes `Simplify` on `σ_{i−1} ◦ (v_i)` with `δ` doubled `t` times until the minimum‑even‑vertex‑distance condition is met (Algorithm 3, PDF p.11 lines 653–664).
3. Add the size‑budget trigger `|σ_{i−1}| ≥ 2k − 2 → Compress` (Algorithm 2, PDF p.10 lines 621–652, line 21).
4. Maintain `O(log_{1+ε}(1/ε)) = O((1/ε)·log(1/ε))` parallel runs of `Reduce` with different guesses of `r` (Theorem 9 proof, PDF p.14 lines 877–891).
5. Enforce the "no three consecutive vertices are collinear" preprocessing (paper §3.1, last paragraph, PDF p.10 lines 609–613).

Currently the repo does **not** do any of (1)–(5); `simplify.cpp` is purely the δ‑simplification from §2.

## 8. Other correctness notes

- **Default parameters**: `DELTA = 200`, `EPSILON = 0.5` (lines 21–22) — these match the paper's convention (ε in (0,1), δ > 0). README says default ε is 0.6; the code says 0.5; README is slightly stale.
- **ASCII-only / file paths**: I did not modify any file (read‑only as requested).
- **Cleanest design choice to recover exact (not approximate) δ-simplification if ever needed**: replace the grid cover with exact ball‑line stabbing (the static minimum‑link path computation); the working storage blows up to O(n) and it stops being a streaming algorithm.

## Summary

The implementation is a faithful, faithful implementation of the paper's `Simplify(ε, δ)` (Algorithm 1, §2 / Theorem 3). Every paper construct has a corresponding code routine (`P`, `conv(G_v)`, `S_a[p]`, `F(S,p)`, `S_{a+1}[p] = conv(G) ∩ F`) with the same constants (GRID = εδ/(2√2), R = (1+ε/2)δ, target bound (1+ε)δ). The only material divergence from the paper text — the finite bounding box used to truncate the otherwise‑unbounded cone `F(S, p)` — is provably safe (Lemma 1 invariant preserved) and necessary for O(ε^(−4)) memory. The (1+ε) approximation is structural (grid discretization), not heuristic, so **no implementation can promise exact `d_F ≤ δ`** in this framework without abandoning the streaming regime. The k‑simplification half of the paper (Algorithms 2 & 3, Theorem 9) is **not implemented** in `simplify.cpp`/`simplify_geometry.h`.
